name: The platforms your child uses
seo_title: Apps Kids Use: A UK Parent's Guide (2026)
seo_description: The apps and platforms UK children use in 2026: what each is for, where the risks sit, and a plain-English guide for each one, from TikTok to Roblox.
h1: The platforms your child is using
lead: Children don't use one app. They move between video, messaging, gaming and AI all day, and the risks often sit in the gaps between them. Here's a map of the main platforms, with a guide for each.
answer: Mostly video apps (YouTube, TikTok), messaging (WhatsApp, Snapchat), games (Roblox, Fortnite) and, increasingly, AI chatbots. Ofcom found phone ownership jumps from 56% of 10-year-olds to 83% of 11-year-olds, so the move to secondary school is when most of this starts.

sections.heading: What parents need to understand
list: It's never one app: a chat that starts in a game often moves to Snapchat or WhatsApp
Features matter more than the app: private messages, live streams and stranger matching carry the most risk
Most apps say 13+, but few check properly, and many children are on them younger
Settings help, but talking helps more

sections.heading: What Ofcom found in 2026
body: In Ofcom's May 2026 research, 56% of 8 to 17-year-olds used AI tools, 55% at least sometimes talked to people they'd only met online, and nearly three-quarters of 11 to 17-year-olds said they'd seen harmful content online.

subsections.heading: YouTube and YouTube Shorts
body: Almost every child watches. Watch for recommendations and the endless Shorts feed. Read the guides: [YouTube](/guides/youtube) and [YouTube Shorts](/guides/youtube-shorts).

subsections.heading: TikTok
body: Short videos picked by the algorithm. Watch for trends, time lost and LIVE. Read the guide: [TikTok](/guides/tiktok).

subsections.heading: Instagram
body: Photos, Reels and messages, with Teen Accounts for under-18s. Watch for comparison and DMs. Read the guide: [Instagram](/guides/instagram).

subsections.heading: X, Pinterest and BeReal
body: X is public and unfiltered; Pinterest is gentler but can lead to body image content; BeReal photos can show where your child is. Read the guides: [X](/guides/x-twitter), [Pinterest](/guides/pinterest) and [BeReal](/guides/bereal).

subsections.heading: WhatsApp
body: Where most group chats live. Watch for group adds and bullying. Read the guide: [WhatsApp](/guides/whatsapp).

subsections.heading: Snapchat
body: Disappearing messages, streaks and Snap Map, and the app most often named in UK grooming cases. Read the guide: [Snapchat](/guides/snapchat).

subsections.heading: Discord
body: Chat servers built around games and interests, with voice chat. Read the guide: [Discord](/guides/discord).

subsections.heading: Roblox
body: Millions of user-made games with chat. Watch for strangers and spending. Read the guide: [Roblox](/guides/roblox).

subsections.heading: Online gaming and voice chat
body: Fortnite, Minecraft, console games and more. Watch for voice chat with strangers and in-game spending. Read the guide: [Online gaming and voice chat](/guides/online-gaming-voice-chat).

sections.heading: AI apps
body: Chatbots such as ChatGPT, Snapchat's My AI and Meta AI, and companion apps such as Character.AI. Watch for children treating them as friends or confidants. Read the guide: [Character.AI](/guides/character-ai).

sections.heading: Apps that worry me most
body: Apps built to connect children with strangers: Wizz, Kik, Chat Hour and Omoggle. If you find one on your child's phone, stay calm and talk. Read the guides: [Wizz](/guides/wizz), [Kik](/guides/kik), [Chat Hour](/guides/chat-hour) and [Omoggle](/guides/omoggle).

sections.heading: What parents can do
body: Ask your child to give you a tour of their phone: which apps, who they talk to, what they love. Then use your device's parental controls to approve new downloads, so a new app becomes a conversation rather than a surprise.
list: "Where do you chat with people you've met online?"
"Is there an app everyone's using that I should know about?"

teachers: Pupils often move between platforms in a single conversation, so a concern raised about one app may involve several. Use this page as a quick reference, and share it with parents ahead of transition to secondary school, when phone ownership jumps.

faq.q: What apps do most children use?
faq.a: YouTube, TikTok, WhatsApp, Snapchat, Instagram and Roblox, plus AI chatbots. Most children use several every day.

faq.q: What age do most UK children get a phone?
faq.a: Ofcom found ownership rises from 56% of 10-year-olds to 83% of 11-year-olds, around the move to secondary school.

faq.q: Which apps are most dangerous for children?
faq.a: Apps designed to connect children with strangers, such as Wizz, Kik, Chat Hour and Omoggle, along with any app's private messages and live streaming.

faq.q: How do I stop my child downloading apps?
faq.a: Turn on Ask to Buy on iPhone or approvals in Google Family Link, so you approve every new download.

help: Worried about something on your child's phone? Childline is free and confidential on [0800 1111](tel:08001111), any time. You are not alone.
sources: Ofcom, "Younger phone owners, the rise of AI, and consumption over creation" (Children's Media Lives and media use research), 21 May 2026
